newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Feb retail sales rose 0.8 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Feb retail sales rose 0.8 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported retail sales rose 0.8 percent in February against an upwardly revised 1.5 percent gain in January.

Excluding autos, sales rose 0.5 percent in February, compared to an upwardly revised 1.4 percent rise in January. Economists in a Reuters survey had expected February sales to rise 0.6 percent overall and 0.7 percent excluding autos.
DAN SETO, ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "The biggest surprise of all is the revision to January."
Seto was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.
MARILYN SCHAJA, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DONALDSON, LUFKIN & JENRETTE SECURITIES CORP: "The numbers overall have probably bolstered the case for a Federal Reserve tightening.

"The retail sales numbers for February were on consensus and not more bothersome for the markets than had been feared, but you have this large January revision. It's not like it was reversed in February; it was compounded."
JOSEPH CARSON, CHIEF FIXED INCOME ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL: "There's no question the consumer sector is accelerating here in the first quarter.

"We thought consumer spending would be 3.0 to 3.5 percent of the quarter and it's probably running four-plus. I think that changes the picture for the Fed; last September when they held off it was because of a weak retail complex where retail sales were almost flat to down over a three-month period going into September, and now you have a rising trend of sales."

ASTRID ADOLFSON, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "There were upward revisions to January and December, and I think that is key. The upward revision suggests that consumers came into the year on a very strong note.
"Taken together with (the jobless claims) numbers that fell, I think we have a strong report, that's why I think the (Fed's) Beige Book (released on Wednesday) was misleading."

DONALD MAUDE, CHIEF U.S. ECONOMIST, SCOTIA CAPITAL MARKETS: "The key was the January revisions ... broad-based, rather than in one specific area. That's probably going to lead to upward revisions to estimates of (growth) for the first quarter by about half a percentage point. We were at 3.5 percent; we're probably moving up to 4.0 percent.
"The (jobless) claims numbers continued to be exceptionally strong. It's been at these levels too long to be excused away as a seasonal quirk. You're looking at the tightest labor market since 1989.
"I would certainly think this brings the Fed back to play at the March 25 meeting."

MARY DENNIS, SENIOR MARKET ECONOMIST, CREDIT SUISSE FIRST BOSTON: "We thought these numbers were very, very strong with the upward revision to January and benefit recipients now at the lowest we've seen in some time.
"Overall, this will give us a pretty solid (growth) number. Net-net, with the revisions (growth) will be up around 3.0 percent."
